content.thinking:
I'm planning the pixel art proportions for a monster truck, working out realistic scale: roughly 5.5m long, 3.4m tall, with tires about 1.7m in diameter sized against a 3.3m track width.

For the texture resolution, I'm setting texel sizes so the paint sheet stays sharp—around 0.05m for the body and finer 0.025m detailing, with a 2048px atlas to keep density comfortable.

Now I'm sketching out the joint hierarchy: a root chassis, four wheel hinges, front steering knuckles parenting the front wheels, and hinged door joints, trying to keep the rig manageable without overcomplicating it with extra suspension or spoiler parts.

For wheels, I'm aligning the hinge axis along X so the cylinder geometry spins correctly, then building each tire from a chunky low-poly cylinder with a painted sidewall decal for tread and lettering, and figuring out whether to merge the lug/tread blocks per wheel to avoid an explosion of separate parts.

Still writing tread geometry...

With 14 lugs at 25.7° spacing, I should align rotation so one lug always points straight down for each wheel, ensuring that lug touches the floor rather than leaving a gap between lugs.

Working through both direction cases, I find that local +Z consistently maps to world up regardless of orientation. Since the lug position depends on local x,z coordinates and down corresponds to local -Z, that places the lug angle at θ = -90 degrees.

I'm checking that the geometry stays consistent since it's built in world space before parenting, and verifying the box corner radius calculation to settle on an outer radius of 0.86 and wheel center height of 0.855.

For each lug box I'm figuring out the rotation that aligns its radial axis using rotateY(-θ), then merging the geometry with that rotation and translating it to the correct radial position based on the box's radial, axial, and tangential dimensions.

For the sidewall, I'm applying cellPaint to the flat faces (normal along ±X) using radial distance from the wheel center to create ring-like cell patterns, rather than trying to overlay a separate decal texture.

I'm adding sidewall shoulder lugs at regular angular intervals for that classic monster-tire protective-block look, then building out the rim: a wide beveled cylinder with metallic paint, bolt ring, and center cap.

Now I'm sizing the overall truck proportions — settling on a half-track of 1.4m giving a total width around 3.75m, a 3.0m wheelbase, and a tire radius of 0.855m for roughly 1.7m diameter wheels, placing the axle height accordingly.

I'm planning the chassis frame dimensions, then designing solid axles with pumpkin differential housings, trailing-arm links, and especially the big signature coilover shocks — angled dampers with helical coil springs built via a spiral sweep path, alternating colored rings for that classic monster truck look.

Working out spiral geometry for shocks...

Actually, I'm reconsidering a safer approach: instead of a parametric spiral, stacking small flat rings (thin cylinders) repeated along the shock length to mimic a pixel-style coil, merged into one part with a single color, which avoids the risk of getting axis/pitch math wrong.

For each shock I'll add a silver rod and dark reservoir cylinder alongside the body, then decide on quantity — going with two shocks per wheel pair (eight total), each built from a handful of merged parts. Next I'll move on to shaping the pickup-style truck body.

For color, I'm leaning toward a vivid orange shell with yellow-white flame decals and dark purple-navy trim plus chrome accents, since the orange should contrast well against the black tires.

Now I'm working out the body placement relative to the wheels—monster truck bodies typically sit raised high above the tires, with the fenders arching over the wheel tops rather than the body intersecting them, so I need the bottom of the body to clear the tire tops by a reasonable margin.

I'm adjusting the body width and half-track so the tires sit just outside the body without clipping, settling on half track 1.45 with body half-width 0.95. Now I'm sketching the pickup silhouette parts in side view, starting with the hood's position along z and y.

I'm thinking of extruding a stepped pixel-art silhouette of the pickup's side profile as a single slab, using the cross product of the extrusion axes to figure out correct centering and thickness along the body's width.

For surface detail, cellPaint can handle side-face patterns like flames, panel lines, and window shapes by mapping cell coordinates to z/y, but I'm now leaning toward building the body from separate boxes instead — a lower body tub and a greenhouse-style cab — for clearer structure, then layering painted patterns onto those surfaces.

For the cab, I'm thinking a stepped pixel-art silhouette with a sloped windshield (4-6 steps at 0.1m increments) would give it that chunky retro look. Windows could be a slightly wider glass slab inset behind the cab's extruded profile so the glass shows through both the side openings and the sloped windshield faces, with the cab body itself in orange surrounding it.

I'm leaning toward a simpler approach: build the windshield as its own tilted thin box with a glass-like pixel texture (dark blue with a diagonal highlight streak) rather than trying to merge geometry, since textured boxes already read well on all faces in this style. I'll stick to boxy primitives throughout, painted with cell-shaded color ramps and pixel textures for detail, and now I need to carefully work out the actual coordinates and palette for the build.

I'm setting up the color constants — orange/flame ramps for fire effects, steel and rubber ramps for mechanical parts, plus accent colors like yellow spring and red — while planning to lean mostly on paints and textures rather than flat colors to stay within the limit. Now I'm starting to define the chassis joint structure, naming the root "chassis" and thinking through whether it needs an explicit role before laying out the rest of the joints.

Next I'm planning the steering knuckles and wheel joints for the front axle, with hinge-type vertical steering joints parented to the chassis and wheel joints attached beneath them, using a left/right naming convention based on sign. I'm also sketching the rear wheel joints, the door hinges (vertical axis, parented to chassis, with window and handle details on the door panel), and considering whether to include a hood or tailgate hinge as optional extras.

Now I'm adding the tailgate joint at the rear of the bed with a horizontal hinge axis, and deciding to skip steering wheel, antenna, and driveshaft joints since the wheels, steering, doors, and tailgate already cover roughly ten joints total. I'm working out how parts should be bound to the nearest joint or explicitly assigned a bone like chassis, and sketching helper functions for creating boxes with consistent color and positioning so I don't have to repeat geometry code for each part.

Now I'm defining the paint functions for the body, planning a base orange ramp shaded by surface normal with dithering noise for texture, plus a flame decal pattern that I want to wrap around the sides and hood using a procedural mask based on position so the flame tongues rise and taper naturally along the body.

Working out the flame tongue math, with layered color bands—dark purple-red outlines, orange-yellow mid, and pale yellow tips—to get a high-contrast pixel-art flame look against the orange body, applied only to the side faces for now.

I'm also adding a navy belt stripe along the top of the lower body, and planning a door decal: a pixel-art number roundel (navy numeral on a white circle) to give the car a racing-livery feel.

Still drawing roundel pixels...

Still mapping out the pattern grid...

Row10 checks out too. Now I need to figure out texture placement and orientation—using a transparent PlaneGeometry for the pixel art so the dots become see-through, and positioning the left door panel facing the +X direction so it reads correctly from the viewer's perspective outside.

For the window glass, I'll use a dark blue gradient pixel texture with light diagonal streaks, applying it to a thin box so it reads correctly on the visible face while keeping the geometry simple. I'm now locking down the coordinate system (y up, z forward) and precise body measurements—wheelbase at z=±1.55, wheel centers at y=0.855 and x=±1.45, with tire radius and width to match.

Now I'm sketching the chassis: steel rails running the length of the frame with crossmembers at regular intervals, plus a tubular cage and support rods connecting the frame to the body up front and rear. I'm also placing the front axle housing as a rod between the wheel hubs, with a boxy differential pumpkin centered on the axle.

I'm adding planetary gear hub boxes at the wheel ends visible through the spokes, connecting them to the steering knuckle up front and chassis in back, plus drive shafts running from the transfer case to each differential and small 4-link suspension rods linking the axles to the frame.

For the shocks, I'm working out placement so they sit vertical near each wheel without clipping into the tire, which spans roughly x 0.96 to 1.94. Mounting the top near the chassis rail and the bottom near the axle gives a shock length around 0.78, and I'm offsetting two shocks per axle end at slightly different x and z positions so they don't overlap.

Now I'm moving on to the body shape itself, planning to define the half-width and build the pickup silhouette — hood, cab, bed — as a stepped side-profile extrusion, figuring out row heights at a 0.1m cell size from the floor up to roughly 3.3m.

Mapping out the profile rows from rear to front: lower body spans the full length from z -2.0 to 2.2 for the first several rows up through y 2.55, where the hood sits, before the shape starts narrowing or sloping toward the front nose.

I'm now puzzling over how to render the pickup bed, which is normally hollow but has to work as a solid extrusion -- considering whether to leave the bed region lower than the cab, cap it with a thin flat "bed floor" face textured as bedliner, or add raised side rails, settling on extruding the bed solid up to a lower height around y 2.35.

I'm laying out the full z-axis cell ranges for bed, cab, and hood sections, figuring out where each row transitions in height (bed roughly y 1.85-2.45, hood region rising to 2.55-2.65, cab greenhouse starting around 2.65), and checking these against the vehicle's real total height so the roof, tires, and floor all line up proportionally.

Now I'm working out the windshield rake by stepping the front edge cells back by one as each row rises, mapping cell indices to z-coordinates, and checking the resulting roof length against a realistic pickup cab proportion (~0.9m roof over 1.5m cab interior) before deciding to shift the cell range to get a better match.

Mapping out the row spans now: full-width bed/cab base for rows 0-5, narrowing to the cab-only width at rows 6-7 since the bed stops at cell 10
